claims.text: Toughness retention or loss in HEAs is governed by the stability and distribution of nanoscale secondary phases within the matrix.
Increasing the volume fraction of brittle secondary phases reduces toughness.
Increasing the connectivity of brittle secondary phases reduces toughness.
A homogeneous single-phase solid solution retains greater toughness than an alloy containing connected brittle secondary phases.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi can serve as a homogenized, single-phase FCC baseline.
Aging time and temperature can be varied to systematically increase the volume fraction of secondary phases such as sigma phase or other intermetallics.
Brittle secondary phases act as crack-initiation sites.
Brittle secondary phases reduce the matrix's ability to undergo plastic deformation.
A single-phase solid solution permits more uniform plastic deformation and greater energy absorption before fracture.
Samples with increased volume fraction and connectivity of brittle secondary phases will exhibit more than a 20% decrease in K_IC or Charpy impact energy relative to the single-phase baseline.
A homogenized HEA with no detectable secondary phases exhibits high toughness.
The proposed behavior is limited to HEAs whose secondary phases are brittle and incoherent with the matrix.
The proposed behavior may not apply when secondary phases are ductile or coherent with the matrix.
The proposed behavior may not apply when the secondary-phase volume fraction is below approximately 1–2%.
The magnitude of toughness reduction depends on secondary-phase type, size, and distribution.
The toughness reduction may be less pronounced when precipitates are nanoscale and well dispersed.
